//mobile: Every key the desktop reads is held here byte-for-byte; `npm run check:manifests` fails the build if it drifts. GitLab is the site worth reading if you want to know why this format is shaped the way it is - it disagrees with everyone else on nearly every axis at once.
tokenHelp: Preferences -> Access tokens, with read_api. read_repository alone is not enough to list merge requests.
//: GitLab uses its own header rather than Authorization.
//endpoints: GitLab addresses a project by a URL-encoded owner/name pair rather than a path, so {owner} and {repo} are separated by %2F here rather than a slash.

endpoints.//comments: The one place a merge request is not an issue with another name: GitLab files their conversations under separate addresses, so both are named. Everywhere else pullRequestComments is absent and comments serves both.
endpoints.//commits: ref_name, not sha or ref - GitLab's own spelling for the branch to list history from.
endpoints.//commit: The commit carries its line totals but not its files. Those are a list of their own at commitFiles, each with its patch in the same diff field a merge request's files use - so there is no raw-diff fallback to name, and none is needed.
endpoints.//readme: GitLab will not serve a file without being told which ref, even for the default branch, so HEAD is named explicitly. The dot in README.md is encoded because the path itself is a single URL segment here.
endpoints.//contents: Two addresses, not one: GitLab lists a directory from repository/tree and reads a file from repository/files, which is why the format has a separate tree endpoint at all. Note {encodedPath} rather than {path} - a file is named by its whole path inside a single URL segment, so src/app/index.tsx has to arrive as src%2Fapp%2Findex.tsx.
endpoints.//notifications: GitLab has no notification inbox; todos are the nearest thing and carry the same three facts a row needs.

//issueStates: GitLab says opened where everyone else says open. Asking it for state=open returns everything rather than failing, so without this the closed filter would quietly do nothing.
//ownerFields: A GitLab group is addressed by a numeric id rather than by name, so both are mapped: full_path is what the user recognises, id is what the create call needs. min_access_level=30 above asks only for groups the user is a developer of or better - the rest are ones they could not create in anyway.
//createRepository: The three ways GitLab differs from everyone else, in one block: one address for both personal and group projects, the group named by a numeric namespace_id in the body rather than in the URL, and privacy spelled as a word instead of a boolean. This is the write-side mirror of the visibility mapping in repositoryFields.
//repositoryFields: Note how little of this matches Gitea: different field names, a nested owner path, and a visibility string instead of a boolean.
//gitCredentials: GitLab wants a fixed username with the token as the password.
//pullRequestFields: A merge request is a pull request under another name. Note iid, not id: the per-project number is what appears in the URL and in the ref, while id is global and would name someone else's merge request entirely.
//issueFields: Same story as merge requests: iid rather than id, description rather than body, and labels that arrive as bare strings with no colour attached.
//commitFields: id, not sha, and the message sits at the top level rather than under a commit object.
//treeFields: GitLab says tree and blob where everyone else says dir and file. The provider normalises the pair, so the manifest only has to name the field.
//changedFileFields: GitLab describes a change with three booleans - new_file, deleted_file, renamed_file - rather than one status word, and counts no lines per file. So status and the counts are deliberately left unmapped: a row says Changed rather than guessing a word, and the provider counts the lines from the patch itself.
//notificationFields: A todo, described as a notification. state is pending until it is acted on, which is the nearest thing GitLab has to unread.
//pullRequestRef: GitLab files merge request heads somewhere else entirely, which is why this is a manifest field and not a constant.
//webUrls: The one place GitLab's website differs in shape from everyone else's: a /-/ between the project and the page. Opening a merge request is a form with its own query parameters rather than a compare page.
